Therapy approaches | Internal Family Systems-informed therapy

Listen to the conflict within, without becoming the conflict.

IFS uses the language of parts to explore competing feelings and protective responses. Learn what that model means, how a session may feel, and why consent and pacing remain essential.

The idea to keep in mind

Parts are a way of describing experience.

A part of you may want to speak up while another wants to avoid conflict. The language is a therapeutic model, not a claim that you contain separate people or a new diagnosis.

Understanding the approach

A protective response may have more than one effect.

Internal Family Systems describes inner experience in terms of parts with different feelings, beliefs, and protective roles. The model also uses Self to describe a compassionate, curious quality of relating to those experiences. These are concepts within the IFS framework, not anatomical structures or conclusions established by an online article.

The approach often asks what a reaction is trying to accomplish, even when its effects are painful. An inner critic, for example, might be understood as trying to prevent rejection by demanding perfection. Understanding that protective intention does not mean agreeing that the criticism is accurate or that harmful behavior should continue.

IFS-informed work draws on this perspective; it does not establish a clinician's certification or use of the complete model. Some people find parts language intuitive, while others prefer a different way of describing internal conflict. The therapist should make the language useful to you rather than require you to adopt it.

Sources ifs psychotherapy

In plain language

Curiosity is not surrender.

You can become interested in the purpose of an urge or belief without treating it as a command. A gentler relationship with an experience can coexist with choosing not to act on it.

A worked example

The application is ready. The submit button still feels impossible.

A fictional example of competing responses around a work opportunity.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

The ambition

Devin wants to apply for a role that fits their interests. They have completed the application and are excited by the possibility.

02

The critic

Another response insists that the application is not good enough. Devin keeps editing, imagining that any imperfection will invite embarrassment.

03

The escape

As the deadline approaches, Devin avoids the application entirely. The avoidance reduces pressure briefly, but the opportunity starts to feel unreachable.

How might an IFS-informed conversation approach this?

Instead of deciding which response is the real Devin, the therapist might explore the concerns each response carries. The critic may be trying to prevent shame; the avoidance may be trying to end an overwhelming struggle. Those are hypotheses to check against Devin's experience, not meanings a therapist can impose.

The work could help Devin notice the responses without becoming completely caught in either. A next step would still need practical judgment about the application. Parts language does not provide a shortcut to deciding what is best, and the example does not instruct anyone to attempt intensive inner work alone.

Sources ifs psychotherapy

Go a little deeper

Terms you may hear, translated into practical questions.

The model is a lens for exploration. The descriptions below are not labels to assign to yourself or another person.

01Protective partsWhat might this response be trying to prevent?Read more +

IFS distinguishes forms of protection, including efforts to keep life controlled and efforts to shut down distress once it rises. The useful question is how a response developed and what it costs now.

Calling a behavior protective does not mean it is harmless, necessary forever, or beyond responsibility. Safety and accountability still apply.

02UnblendingCan you notice the experience without being completely taken over by it?Read more +

Unblending is IFS language for gaining some perspective on a part's thoughts or feelings. A person might move from being entirely identified with self-criticism to noticing that self-criticism is present.

This is not supposed to mean numbing, dissociating, or suppressing emotion. A clinician should distinguish helpful perspective from feeling disconnected or overwhelmed.

03Curiosity toward vulnerabilityWhat needs care, and what pace is tolerable?Read more +

Within the model, protective patterns may surround vulnerable experiences. Work with those experiences should be gradual, consent-based, and appropriate to the person's stability and goals.

A therapist should not treat an image, sensation, or inner dialogue as proof that a historical event occurred. Exploration is different from verifying memory.

04A different internal relationshipCan competing needs be heard without a winner-takes-all struggle?Read more +

The goal is not to eliminate unwanted parts or force them to agree with the therapist. The model emphasizes a less polarized relationship with internal experience.

You can tell a clinician that a metaphor does not fit. Care can use ordinary language about feelings, beliefs, and impulses instead.

Sources ifs psychotherapy

Inside the work

Pacing is part of the method, not an obstacle to it.

01

Agree on language and purpose

Start with the difficulty that brought you to therapy. The clinician explains the parts perspective and checks whether it is meaningful and comfortable for you.

02

Notice a present response

Attention may turn to a current thought, urge, feeling, or pattern. There is no requirement to begin with the most painful experience.

03

Explore with permission

The therapist may ask what the response fears or needs while monitoring whether the work remains manageable. You can pause or decline an exercise.

04

Reconnect with daily life

The session should return to present circumstances and practical goals. Insight is considered alongside choices, relationships, and functioning outside therapy.

Sources ifs psychotherapy

Fit, choice and limitations

A model should never overrule your experience.

Not a diagnosis of multiple identities

Everyday parts language is not a diagnosis of dissociative identity disorder or evidence of separate personalities. Complex dissociative symptoms require appropriate assessment rather than a casual interpretation of a metaphor.

Not proof about the past

Inner images and sensations can be meaningful experiences without establishing historical facts. Care should avoid suggesting certainty about events that have not been independently established.

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

Must I visualize parts or use special names?

No. Ask how the clinician adapts the language and exercises. Some people prefer to describe a familiar feeling, belief, or impulse without imagery or personification. You are not failing therapy because a metaphor is unhelpful.

Does the therapist try to get rid of parts?

The IFS model emphasizes understanding and changing the relationship with parts rather than expelling them. What changes might be a role, belief, or protective strategy. This is the model's framing, not a requirement to experience yourself in that way.

Will I have to revisit trauma?

Discuss the purpose, pacing, alternatives, and your right to pause before any difficult material. Listing IFS-informed therapy does not establish a promise about trauma treatment or a particular sequence of interventions.

Can this fit with practical behavior work?

It can be discussed as part of an integrated plan. For example, understanding the fear behind avoidance does not replace deciding how to respond to the situation. The clinician should explain how reflective and practical parts of care connect.

What happens if I feel overwhelmed or disconnected?

Tell the clinician so the work can stop or change and your immediate needs can be assessed. An exercise is not beneficial simply because it is intense. Do not use this webpage as a guide for intensive self-directed trauma processing.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
